headline: FTSE 100 edges higher on Friday after gilt sell-off but is on course for its worst week since April

terms.meaning: The return investors demand for lending to the UK government; a higher yield means higher borrowing costs
An index of the 100 biggest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange
The government minister in charge of taxes and spending

levels.headline: FTSE 100 edges higher on Friday after gilt sell-off but is on course for its worst week since April
levels.body:
London's FTSE 100 edged up 24 points, or 0.23%, to close at 10,452 on Friday 2 October, recovering a little after Thursday's 1.7% fall to 10,428.27. Even so, the index was on course for its sharpest weekly drop since April.
The relief came as oil prices and UK government borrowing costs eased. The 10-year gilt yield fell to about 5.33% after the previous day's sharp rise, and the 30-year yield, which briefly passed 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998, also slipped back. Sterling had weakened by 0.43% to $1.3206 on Thursday. Investors have been unsettled by rising bond yields around the world and by the standoff between the United States and Iran.
The moves matter for the public finances. Higher gilt yields raise the interest the government pays on its debt, and have cut the room Chancellor John Healey has to meet his fiscal targets to about £13 billion, from £23.6 billion at the Spring Statement, before his Budget on 28 October. Markets also expect the Bank of England, which held Bank Rate at 3.75% in September, to raise rates over the coming year.
levels.why: Government borrowing costs shape the Budget and can feed through to mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: UK shares steady on Friday after a sharp fall, but the week is still the worst since April
levels.body:
The FTSE 100, the index of the 100 biggest companies listed in London, rose 0.23% on Friday 2 October to close at 10,452. That was a small recovery after a 1.7% fall on Thursday, and the index was still heading for its biggest weekly drop since April.
The market steadied because oil prices and the cost of government borrowing both eased. The 10-year gilt yield, the interest rate on UK government debt, fell to about 5.33%. On Thursday the 30-year yield had briefly gone above 6%, a level not seen since 1998. Investors have been worried about rising borrowing costs around the world and the standoff between the US and Iran.
This matters because higher yields mean a bigger interest bill for the government. Chancellor John Healey now has about £13 billion of room to meet his fiscal targets, down from £23.6 billion in the spring. He presents his Budget on 28 October. Markets also think the Bank of England, which kept its rate at 3.75% in September, may raise it over the next year.
levels.why: A bigger interest bill leaves the Chancellor less room and can raise the cost of loans for everyone.

levels.headline: London shares recover a little on Friday, but it has still been a bad week
levels.body:
London's main share index, the FTSE 100, went up by 0.23% on Friday to 10,452. That is a small bounce after it fell by 1.7% on Thursday. Over the whole week it has still dropped by more than in any week since April.
The market was calmer because the price of oil and the cost of government borrowing both came down a bit. The government borrows by selling bonds called gilts, and pays interest on them. On Thursday the interest on a 30-year gilt went above 6% for the first time since 1998. Worries about the US and Iran, and about rising borrowing costs across the world, have made investors nervous.
When the government pays more interest, it has less left to spend. The Chancellor, John Healey, says what he will do with taxes and spending on 28 October. He has about £13 billion of spare room now, down from £23.6 billion earlier this year. The Bank of England has kept its rate at 3.75%, but investors think it may go up.
levels.why: Higher interest on government debt leaves less money for other things and can mean tax rises.

levels.headline: UK shares rise a little on Friday after a big fall, but the week has been poor
levels.body:
Share prices in London went up a little on Friday. The FTSE 100, a list of the 100 biggest companies in London, rose 0.23% to 10,452. On Thursday it had fallen 1.7%, so this week is still the worst for shares since April.

He will make a speech on taxes and spending on 28 October. He has less spare room than before, so some people expect taxes to rise.
levels.why: The government's interest bill affects how much it can spend and how much tax people pay.

levels.headline: UK shares edge up on Friday, but it has still been a rough week

levels.headline: UK share prices bounce back slightly, but the week has been tough

levels.why: The government's money problems can end up changing what people pay in tax.

levels.headline: Shares in London go up a little on Friday after a bad week
levels.body:
Share prices in London went up a little on Friday. The FTSE 100 is a list of the biggest 100 companies in London. It rose by 0.23%. That is a small gain. On Thursday it fell by much more, so the week has still been a bad one.

levels.headline: Shares in London rise a little, but it has been a bad week

levels.headline: Share prices go up a little after a bad week

levels.headline: Shares go up a tiny bit, but the week was bumpy

headline: Burnham promises a "new path" and a big expansion of public services in first conference speech as PM

terms.meaning: When the state, rather than private companies, owns a service such as water or energy
The rule that the state pension rises each year by the highest of wage growth, inflation or 2.5%
The amount a person can earn each year before paying income tax, currently £12,570

levels.headline: Burnham promises a "new path" and a big expansion of public services in first conference speech as PM
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham used his first Labour conference speech in Liverpool on Tuesday 29 September to promise a break with what he called the direction of the past 40 years. He said Britain had been on the wrong path for a long time and pledged to build a new economy and a new politics. The hour-long speech covered healthcare, pensions, electoral reform, affordable housing and publicly owned utilities, and drew several standing ovations.
Among the specific pledges, he said low-income pensioners would not pay income tax in the current Parliament, and that his party intends to make it easier for young people to buy a home by reducing the deposit they need. He also set out plans to "rewire" the state, including devolution and Britain's relationship with Europe, and became emotional when speaking about keeping the United Kingdom together. Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July.
Supporters see a bold change of direction after the party's difficult year. Critics are likely to ask how the plans will be paid for, at a time when government borrowing costs are rising and the Chancellor, John Healey, faces a tight Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It shows what the new Prime Minister wants to do, and the cost will be tested at the Budget.

levels.headline: Burnham promises a new path for Britain in his first conference speech as Prime Minister

levels.headline: Andy Burnham sets out a "new path" for Britain at Labour conference
levels.body:
At the Labour conference in Liverpool on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham made his first big speech since taking over from Sir Keir Starmer in July. He said Britain had been on the wrong path for a long time, and he promised to break with the direction of the last 40 years. The speech lasted about an hour and got several standing ovations.

levels.headline: Burnham promises a new direction for Britain and more public services
levels.body:

levels.why: It tells us what the new Prime Minister wants to do, and whether there is enough money to do it.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister promises a new path for the country

levels.why: Plans cost money, so the Budget will show which ones can really happen.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister has a plan for a "new path"

headline: Burnham says Brexit has done "more harm than good" and promises a debate on closer EU ties

terms.meaning: A group of countries that trade with each other without tariffs or border checks
An agreement where countries charge the same taxes on goods from outside the group and trade freely inside it
Changing the way votes are counted to decide who wins elections

levels.headline: Burnham says Brexit has done "more harm than good" and promises a debate on closer EU ties
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the Labour conference in Liverpool on Tuesday that Brexit has done "more harm than good". He pointed to weak economic growth and to a lack of the control over immigration that was promised, and said the UK had lost some control over its economy and its borders.
He said Britain needed to decide what its long-term relationship with Europe should look like, and that he would set out different options and seek a consensus on the way forward. It is understood the options could include rejoining the single market, rejoining the customs union, or even rejoining the EU. He did not commit to any one of them. He also promised to keep the UK together and spoke about electoral reform.
The remarks are likely to please many Labour members, while parties that backed the 2016 vote to leave may oppose them. Any move towards the single market or customs union would also need to be agreed with the EU and could be controversial with voters.
levels.why: It reopens the biggest question in British politics since 2016 and could shape trade, prices and immigration.

He also spoke about keeping the UK together and about changing the voting system.
Many Labour members may welcome this, while parties that backed the 2016 vote to leave may oppose it. Any move closer to the EU would need the EU's agreement and could divide voters.
levels.why: It reopens a huge political question and could affect trade, prices and immigration.

levels.headline: Burnham says Brexit has done more harm than good

At the Labour conference on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Brexit has done "more harm than good". He said the country needs to decide what its long-term link with Europe should be, and that he will set out options and try to reach agreement. Those options could include rejoining the single market, which lets countries trade without taxes at the border, or the customs union. They could even include rejoining the EU. He did not pick one.
Many Labour members may welcome this. Parties that backed the 2016 vote to leave may oppose it. Any change would also need the EU to agree.
levels.why: It could lead to big changes in how the UK trades and works with Europe.

levels.headline: Burnham says leaving the EU has done more harm than good
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, told his party's conference on Tuesday that Brexit has done "more harm than good". Brexit is the name for the UK leaving the European Union in 2020. He said the economy has grown slowly since then. He also said the promise of more control over immigration has not come true.
He said the country must decide how close it wants to be to Europe in the long term. He will set out some choices and try to get people to agree. The choices could include going back into the single market, which is a group of countries that trade freely with each other. They might even include joining the EU again. He has not picked one yet.
Many Labour members may like this idea. Parties that wanted to leave may not. The EU would also have to agree to any change.
levels.why: It reopens a big debate that could change trade, prices and who can move to the UK.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Brexit has not worked well
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said on Tuesday that Brexit has done more harm than good. Brexit is when the UK left the European Union, a group of countries in Europe that work together. He said the country's money has grown slowly since then. He also said the UK did not get all the control over immigration that was promised.
He said the UK must choose how close to be to Europe. He will share some choices and ask people to agree. One choice could be to join a group of countries that trade freely with each other. Another could be to join the EU again. He has not picked one.
Some people like this idea. Other parties do not, because they wanted to leave. The EU would also need to say yes.
levels.why: It could change how the UK trades and works with its neighbours.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister thinks leaving the EU has caused problems
levels.body:
The EU is a group of countries in Europe that work together. A few years ago the UK left it. This is called Brexit. On Tuesday the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said he thinks it did more harm than good. He said the country has not grown richer as fast as it hoped. He said the UK did not get all the control over immigration that was promised. Immigration is when people move to a new country to live.
He now wants the country to decide how close to be to Europe. He will list some choices. One could be trading freely with those countries again. Another could be joining the EU again. He has not picked one.
Some people agree with him. Others do not, because they wanted to leave. The EU would have to say yes as well.
levels.why: The UK might change how close it is to its neighbours in Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says the UK leaving Europe's club was a mistake
levels.body:
Some years ago, the UK left a group of European countries called the EU. Think of it like leaving a club. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said on Tuesday that leaving did more harm than good. He thinks the country did not get richer as quickly as people hoped.
He wants everyone to talk about how close the UK should be to its neighbours now. There could be a few choices. We could trade more freely with them, like swapping stickers with no fuss. Or we could join the club again. He has not picked yet.
Some people agree with him. Some do not, because they were glad to leave. The club would also need to say yes.
levels.why: The UK could end up closer to the countries around it, which might change what we buy and sell.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to talk about our neighbours in Europe
levels.body:
The UK is a country, and next to it are other countries in Europe. A while ago, our country left a group that many of them belong to. The group is like a club. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said that leaving was not a good idea. He thinks it caused more problems than good things.
Now he wants people to talk about it. He wants us to think about how friendly the UK should be with its neighbours. We could share and trade more with them. We could even join the club again. He has not decided yet.
Some people agree with him, and some do not. It is fine to have different ideas. Everyone gets to talk about it.
levels.why: Big choices about friends and neighbours take time, and many people have a say.

levels.headline: Some people think the UK should be friendlier with its neighbours
