The UK is a country, and it has neighbours in Europe. A few years ago the UK left a group of European countries, called the EU. Think of it like leaving a club. On Tuesday the leader of the country, called the Prime Minister, said he thinks leaving did more harm than good. His name is Andy Burnham.
He did not say what we should do next. He said we should talk about it. We could trade more with our neighbours, like swapping things with a friend. Or we could join the club again. Nothing has been decided.
Some people agree with him and some do not. That is fine. In a country, many people get to share what they think.
levels.why: It is a big choice, and many people will have a say.

levels.headline: The leader says to talk about being friends with other countries
levels.body:
Our country, the UK, has neighbours. Some years ago, the UK left a club of European countries. The leader of the country is called the Prime Minister. He is Andy Burnham. On Tuesday he said he thinks leaving was not a good idea.
He wants everyone to talk about it. Maybe we could become closer friends with our neighbours again. Maybe we could share and trade more. He has not decided yet. The other countries would need to say yes, too.
Some people agree, and some do not. In a country, lots of people share their ideas. Then the grown-ups choose together.
levels.why: Choosing together takes time, and everyone gets to share ideas.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August, a five-month high, as fuel prices climb

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time, so your money buys less
Inflation leaving out food and fuel, whose prices jump around a lot
How fast prices are rising for things like haircuts, restaurant meals and hotels

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August, a five-month high, as fuel prices climb
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, up from 3.0% in July and a five-month high, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 16 September. The figure matched what economists had expected. Sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices were the main push upwards, helped by higher airfares, particularly for long-haul journeys.
Underlying pressures were calmer. Core inflation, which leaves out volatile items such as food and fuel, held at 2.6% for a fourth month in a row, and services inflation, which the Bank of England watches closely as a sign of price pressure at home, stayed at 3.4%. That suggests the recent rise comes mostly from energy costs rather than from wages and domestic demand.
The numbers came a day before the Bank of England's September rate decision. Goldman Sachs expects headline inflation to peak at 3.9% in early 2027, so households may face rising bills for some time, with the Iran conflict keeping oil prices high.
levels.why: Higher inflation means everyday costs rise faster than many people's pay, and it affects interest rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.1% in August as petrol and diesel get dearer
levels.body:
UK inflation, the yearly rise in prices, reached 3.1% in August, up from 3.0% in July and the highest for five months, the Office for National Statistics said on 16 September. That was in line with forecasts. Higher petrol and diesel prices were the biggest reason, with dearer airfares, especially long-haul flights, also adding to the rise.
Underlying inflation was steadier. Core inflation, which strips out food and fuel because they swing so much, stayed at 2.6% for the fourth month running. Services inflation, which the Bank of England watches as a sign of price pressure at home, was unchanged at 3.4%. The rise therefore looks mainly like an energy story.
The release came a day before the Bank of England's rate decision. Goldman Sachs expects inflation to peak at 3.9% in early 2027. With the conflict involving Iran keeping oil prices high, households may see costs rising for some months.
levels.why: Prices rising faster than pay makes life dearer and shapes what the Bank of England does with interest rates.

levels.headline: UK prices rose 3.1% in the year to August, driven by fuel costs
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.1% higher in August than a year earlier, the Office for National Statistics reported. That is up from 3.0% in July and is the highest for five months. Economists had expected the figure. Petrol and diesel got much dearer, and flights, especially long ones, cost more as well.
Some measures were calmer. Core inflation, which leaves out food and fuel, stayed at 2.6% for a fourth month. Services inflation, which covers things like restaurants and hotels and which the Bank of England watches closely, was 3.4%, the same as before. So the jump mostly comes from energy prices rather than from pay or demand at home.
The figures came a day before the Bank of England decided on interest rates. Goldman Sachs thinks inflation could reach 3.9% in early 2027, so bills may keep rising while oil stays expensive.
levels.why: If prices rise faster than wages, people can afford less, and rates may stay high.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are rising faster: 3.1% in the year to August
levels.body:
Inflation is the rate at which prices go up. In the UK it was 3.1% in the year to August. That is a little higher than July, when it was 3.0%, and it is the highest for five months. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, shared the figure. Experts had guessed it would be this number.
The main reason was fuel. Petrol and diesel cost a lot more. Plane tickets, especially for long trips, cost more too. Other measures stayed calm. Core inflation, which leaves out food and fuel, was 2.6% for the fourth month. Prices for services, like a haircut or a hotel, were rising at 3.4%, the same as before.
A forecast from Goldman Sachs says inflation could hit 3.9% early next year. Oil is expensive because of the conflict involving Iran, so bills may keep climbing for a while.
levels.why: Things cost more each month, and that affects family budgets and interest rates.

levels.headline: UK prices rose by 3.1% in a year, mostly because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices rise. In the UK, prices in August were 3.1% higher than a year before. In July the figure was 3.0%, so it has crept up. It is the highest for five months, but it is what experts expected.
Fuel is the main cause. Petrol and diesel cost a lot more. Flights, especially long ones, cost more too. Other prices are rising more slowly. If you leave out food and fuel, which change a lot, prices rose 2.6%, the same as for the last four months. That tells us the rise is mostly about energy, not about everything.
A bank called Goldman Sachs thinks inflation could reach 3.9% early next year. Oil is dear because of the conflict involving Iran, so some bills may keep rising for a while.
levels.why: Rising prices make everyday life cost more, especially if pay does not keep up.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, mainly because petrol and diesel cost more
levels.body:
Inflation means that prices go up over time. In August, prices in the UK were 3.1% higher than a year before. In July the rise was 3.0%. This is the biggest rise for five months. People who study the numbers had expected it. The reason was mainly the price of petrol and diesel. Plane tickets for long trips cost more too.
Not everything went up faster. If you leave out food and fuel, which change a lot, prices rose 2.6%. That has stayed the same for four months. Prices for services, such as a haircut or a night in a hotel, rose 3.4%, also the same as before.
One bank, Goldman Sachs, thinks the rise could reach 3.9% early next year. Oil is dear because of a conflict that involves Iran, so costs may stay high for a while.
levels.why: Higher prices make weekly shopping and travel cost more.

levels.headline: Things in the shops and at the petrol station cost more than a year ago
levels.body:
When prices go up, we call it inflation. In August, things in the UK cost 3.1% more than they did a year before. That means something that cost £100 last year costs about £103 now. In July the rise was a bit smaller, at 3.0%. It is the biggest rise for five months.
The main reason is that petrol and diesel cost more. Plane tickets cost more too. Other prices are rising slowly. If you leave out food and fuel, which jump around a lot, the rise is 2.6%, the same as for four months.
A bank called Goldman Sachs thinks prices could rise by 3.9% early next year. Oil is dear because of a conflict that involves Iran, so some bills may keep going up.
levels.why: If prices rise faster than pay, families can buy a little less than before.

levels.headline: Prices keep creeping up, mostly because fuel costs more
levels.body:
When you go to the shop, you pay a price. Over time, prices tend to rise. This is called inflation. In August, things cost 3.1% more than a year earlier. For example, a £100 shopping trip last year costs about £103 now. In July the rise was a little smaller.
Petrol and diesel are the main reason. Car fuel costs a lot more. So do plane tickets for long trips. Other things are rising more slowly. The experts who count prices say the rise is mostly about fuel, not about everything.
Some people who study money think prices could rise even more early next year. Oil is dear because of a conflict that involves Iran. That means some bills could go up.
levels.why: It means your pocket money, or your parents' pay, buys a little less than before.

levels.headline: Things cost a bit more than last year, especially fuel
levels.body:
Do you remember what a chocolate bar cost last year? Prices go up slowly over time. That is called inflation. Over the last year, prices in the UK went up by about 3 pennies for every £1. The rise is a little bigger than it was a month ago.
Fuel is the main reason. Petrol and diesel make cars go, and they cost more now. Plane tickets cost more too. Most other things are going up more slowly.
People who study money think prices could keep going up for a few months. Oil is dear because of a conflict that involves another country, Iran. That is why some bills may go up. Families are watching carefully and trying to save.
levels.why: When prices go up, your money buys a little less than before.

levels.headline: Some things cost a little more than before
levels.body:
Think about your favourite sweet. Last year it cost some pennies. Now it might cost a penny or two more. This is called prices going up. Grown-ups use a big word for it: inflation.
This year, prices went up by about 3 pennies for every £1. It is a small rise, but it adds up. The main thing that got dearer is fuel. Fuel is what makes cars and planes go. Fuel costs more because of a fight far away.
Grown-ups are watching to see if prices keep rising. If they do, families may need to save a bit more. It is like when your pocket money stays the same but the sweets cost more. You can buy a bit less.
levels.why: Your money buys a little less when prices go up.

headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences mortgage and savings rates
The nine-member group at the Bank that votes on interest rates
One hundredth of a percentage point; 25 basis points is 0.25%

levels.headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 on 17 September to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%, the sixth meeting in a row at which rates were left unchanged. Three members, Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene, wanted a quarter-point rise to 4%.
The decision came as the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank have both raised their rates in recent weeks, and after UK inflation climbed to 3.1% in August. The Bank said it expects inflation to reach around 3.75% in the last three months of 2026 and slightly above 4% in early 2027, and judged that the risks to inflation are tilted to the upside, more so than in July.
It also warned that rates may need to rise if the conflict in the Middle East continues and higher energy prices lead to more persistent inflation. The next decision is on 5 November. For households, that means mortgage and savings rates could come under upward pressure rather than fall, and markets will watch the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: The Bank's decisions affect mortgage costs, savings returns and the cost of loans for firms.

levels.headline: Bank of England keeps rates at 3.75% but three members want a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 to leave Bank Rate at 3.75%. It was the sixth meeting in a row without a change. Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene voted to raise it by a quarter of a percentage point, to 4%.
The decision followed rate rises by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, and a jump in UK inflation to 3.1% in August. The Bank expects inflation of around 3.75% in the final three months of 2026 and a little over 4% in early 2027. It said the risks to its outlook lean upwards, more than they did in July.
The Bank warned that rates may have to go up if the conflict in the Middle East continues and higher energy prices make inflation stick. The next decision is on 5 November. That could keep pressure on mortgage and savings rates.
levels.why: It shapes what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England leaves rates at 3.75%, with three votes for a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England decided to keep its main interest rate, Bank Rate, at 3.75%. Six members of its nine-person committee voted for that, and three voted for a rise to 4%. It was the sixth meeting in a row without a change. The three who wanted a rise were Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene.
The US and the eurozone have both raised their rates recently, and UK inflation has gone up to 3.1%. The Bank thinks inflation will reach about 3.75% by the end of the year and just over 4% early next year. It said the risks are more on the upside than they were in July.
The Bank said rates might need to go up if the conflict in the Middle East continues and energy prices keep inflation high. The next meeting is on 5 November. Mortgage and savings rates may stay under pressure until then.
levels.why: It affects the cost of home loans and the interest people earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England keeps interest rates the same, but some want a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England sets a main interest rate, called Bank Rate. It affects what people pay on loans and mortgages, and what they earn on savings. The Bank has kept it at 3.75%. Six of the nine people who vote wanted no change. Three wanted to raise it to 4%.
Prices are rising faster now, at 3.1% a year. The Bank thinks prices will rise even faster by the end of the year. The US and the eurozone have both raised their rates lately. Energy prices are high because of the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank said it may raise rates if the conflict goes on and energy prices keep prices high. It will decide again on 5 November. Until then, mortgage and savings rates may stay high.
levels.why: A higher rate makes loans dearer, but it can mean better pay on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England keeps interest rates at 3.75%, but a rise could come
levels.body:
The Bank of England sets the UK's main interest rate. It affects what people pay on loans and mortgages and what they earn on savings. This time the rate stayed at 3.75%. Six of the nine members who vote wanted no change, and three wanted a rise to 4%.
The Bank is worried about prices. Inflation is 3.1% and the Bank thinks it will go up to about 3.75% by the end of the year. The US and the countries that use the euro have already raised their rates. Energy is dear because of the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank said it may raise rates if energy prices keep inflation high. It will decide again on 5 November.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay at 3.75%, but they might go up soon
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the UK's money. It sets an interest rate. Interest is the price of borrowing money, and also the reward for saving it. The rate is now 3.75%, and it has not changed. Nine people vote on it. Six wanted no change. Three wanted a small rise.
The Bank is worried that prices are rising too fast. They are going up by 3.1% a year. The Bank thinks they may go up by even more soon. Fuel and energy are dear because of the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank said it may raise rates if that goes on. It will vote again on 5 November. Until then, people with a mortgage, which is a loan for a house, may keep paying quite a lot.
levels.why: Interest rates change what people pay on loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England says rates stay the same for now
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a very big bank. Its job is to keep prices steady. It has a main interest rate. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The rate is 3.75%. The Bank left it the same this time. Nine people voted. Six said keep it. Three said put it up.
Prices are going up a bit faster now. That is why some of the voters wanted a rise. Prices can go up when fuel is dear. Fuel is dear because of a fight far away in the Middle East.
The Bank said it may raise the rate if prices keep rising. It will meet again on 5 November. If it goes up, borrowing will cost more.
levels.why: When rates go up, loans cost more and savings can earn more.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay the same for now, but they could go up in November
levels.body:
Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The Bank of England chooses the main interest rate for the UK. It is 3.75% now. On 17 September the Bank decided to leave it as it is. Nine people voted. Six wanted no change. Three wanted a small rise.
The Bank is watching prices closely. They are rising by 3.1% a year, which is faster than before. The Bank thinks they could rise faster still by the end of the year. Fuel and energy cost more because of the conflict in the Middle East.
If prices keep rising, the Bank might raise the rate. It will meet again on 5 November. Until then, many people with a mortgage, which is a loan to buy a home, will wait to see what happens.
levels.why: When the rate changes, home loans and savings change too.

levels.headline: The people who look after money decide to keep a rate the same
levels.body:
The Bank of England is where the country's money is looked after. The people there choose a number called the interest rate. When you save money in a bank, you get a little extra. That is interest. When you borrow, you pay a little extra. That is interest too. The number is now 3.75%. The Bank decided not to change it. Three people wanted it a bit higher.
Prices are going up a bit faster now, so the Bank is watching closely. Fuel costs more because of a fight far away. If prices keep going up, the Bank may raise the number.
It will meet again on 5 November. Grown-ups with loans will be watching. A loan for a house costs more when the number goes up.
levels.why: The number changes how much extra grown-ups pay on loans and get on savings.

levels.headline: Grown-ups at the bank decide to leave the number the same
levels.body:
Do you save pocket money in a piggy bank? Some people put money in a real bank. The bank gives them a little extra for keeping it there. The extra is called interest. If someone borrows money, they pay extra back. A group at a big bank, called the Bank of England, chooses how big the extra is. This time they chose to keep it the same.
Three people in the group wanted it to go up. They are worried that prices are going up too fast. A higher number would help slow prices down, but it makes loans cost more.
They will meet again on 5 November. Until then, grown-ups with loans will be watching.
levels.why: Small changes in this number can change what families pay each month.

headline: UK economy grew 0.4% in July, beating forecasts, though unemployment is 4.9%

terms.meaning: Gross domestic product, the total value of goods and services a country produces
The share of people able and looking for work who do not have a job
Businesses that sell services, such as shops, restaurants, banks and hotels

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.4% in July, beating forecasts, though unemployment is 4.9%
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.4% in July 2026, well above the 0% economists had expected, the Office for National Statistics said on 11 September. It followed growth of 0.3% in June and none in May. Services grew 0.4%, production 0.2% and construction 0.1%. Over the three months to July, GDP was 0.4% higher than in the three months to April, the eighth three-month period in a row of growth, and it was 1.6% above July last year.
The jobs market is softer. The ONS said on 15 September that unemployment was 4.9% in May to July, up 0.2 percentage points on a year earlier but largely unchanged on the latest quarter. About 1.78 million people aged 16 and over were out of work, 83,000 more than a year before.
So the economy is growing steadily, but not fast enough to bring unemployment down. At the same time inflation is rising and borrowing costs are climbing, which could weigh on growth in the months ahead.
levels.why: It shows how the economy is doing and whether jobs and pay are likely to improve.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.4% in July, more than expected, while unemployment stays at 4.9%
levels.body:
The UK economy grew 0.4% in July, the Office for National Statistics said on 11 September. Economists had forecast no growth. June had grown 0.3% and May had been flat. Services rose 0.4%, production 0.2% and construction 0.1%. In the three months to July the economy was 0.4% bigger than in the three months to April, the eighth growth period in a row, and 1.6% bigger than a year ago.
The jobs market is weaker. Figures on 15 September showed unemployment at 4.9% in May to July, up 0.2 percentage points from a year earlier but little changed on the last quarter. About 1.78 million people were unemployed, 83,000 more than a year before.
The economy is expanding steadily, but not quickly enough to cut unemployment. Rising inflation and higher borrowing costs could slow growth later in the year.
levels.why: It tells us whether the economy is healthy enough to protect jobs and incomes.

levels.headline: UK economy grew by 0.4% in July, but 4.9% of workers are unemployed
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.4% in July, the Office for National Statistics reported. Experts had expected it to stay flat. The economy grew by 0.3% in June and did not grow in May. The service industries, such as shops and hotels, grew by 0.4%. Factories and other production grew by 0.2%, and construction by 0.1%. Compared with a year ago, the economy is 1.6% bigger.
Jobs figures were less happy. The unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July. That is 0.2 points higher than a year before. About 1.78 million people were out of work, which is 83,000 more than a year earlier.
So the economy is growing, but not by enough to bring unemployment down. Higher prices and borrowing costs could slow growth over the coming months.
levels.why: It affects whether people can find work and whether pay keeps up with prices.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew in July, but more people are out of work than last year
levels.body:
GDP is the total amount a country makes and sells. In July, the UK's GDP grew by 0.4%. Experts had expected no growth, so it was a nice surprise. Shops, hotels and other service businesses grew by 0.4%. Factories grew by 0.2% and building by 0.1%. The economy is now 1.6% bigger than a year ago.
Jobs news was not as good. Unemployment was 4.9% in the three months to July. That means about 5 out of every 100 people who want a job do not have one. It is slightly higher than a year ago. About 1.78 million people are without work, which is 83,000 more than last year.
The economy is growing, but not fast enough to create many new jobs. Higher prices and borrowing costs could slow it down.
levels.why: It shows if the country is getting richer and if people can get jobs.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew more than expected in July, but unemployment is 4.9%
levels.body:
The economy is all the things a country makes, buys and sells. In July the UK economy grew by 0.4%. Experts had expected no growth, so it was a good surprise. Shops, hotels and other services grew by 0.4%. Factories and building grew a little. Over the year the economy has grown by 1.6%.
The jobs news was not as strong. The unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July. That is slightly higher than a year ago. About 1.78 million people had no job, which is 83,000 more than a year before.
So the economy is growing, but not quickly enough to bring unemployment down. Rising prices and higher borrowing costs could slow growth in the months ahead.
levels.why: It shows whether there will be enough jobs and whether pay can keep up with prices.

levels.headline: The UK's money-making grew in July, but jobs are harder to find than last year
levels.body:
The economy is all the buying and selling in a country. In July it grew by 0.4%. Experts had thought it would not grow at all, so this was a good surprise. Shops, hotels and banks did well. Factories and builders grew a little as well. Over the year, the economy has grown 1.6%.
There was less happy news about jobs. About 5 in every 100 people who want to work do not have a job. That is a bit more than last year. In all, about 1.78 million people are looking for work.
So the economy is growing, but jobs are not growing fast. Prices are going up and borrowing is getting dearer, which could slow things down.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and pay, but not always right away.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a bit in July, but some people still cannot find work
levels.body:
The economy is all the things people make, buy and sell. In July, the UK economy grew by about half a percent. Experts thought it would stay the same, so this was a nice surprise. Shops, cafes and hotels did well. People who build things did a little better too.
But there is another side. About 5 out of every 100 people who want a job cannot find one. That is a few more than last year. That is about 1.78 million people.
So the country is making more, but not enough new jobs. Prices going up and loans costing more could slow things down in the next months.
levels.why: If the economy grows, there can be more jobs and better pay, but it takes time.

levels.headline: The UK made and sold more in July, but jobs are harder to find
levels.body:
Think of the economy as everything people make and sell, like food, haircuts and cars. In July the UK made and sold about 0.4% more than the month before. Experts had thought it would stay the same, so this was a good surprise. Shops, cafes, hotels and banks did well.
But about 5 out of every 100 people who want a job could not find one. That is a bit more than last year. In all, about 1.78 million people were looking for work.
So the news is mixed. The country is doing a bit better, but there are not enough new jobs. Prices are rising and loans are getting dearer, which could make things harder for families.
levels.why: It shows how well the country is doing and how easy it is to find work.

levels.headline: The country made a bit more in July, but some people have no job
levels.body:
Think of the country as one big shop. If more people buy and sell things, the shop does better. In July the UK shop did a bit better than expected. Cafes, hotels and shops sold more. Builders made a bit more too.
But not everyone has a job. About 5 out of every 100 grown-ups who want to work do not have one. That is a few more than last year. Finding a job can be hard.
So the news is mixed. The country is doing a bit better, but jobs are still hard to find. Prices are rising too, which could make things harder for families.
levels.why: When businesses do well, there can be more jobs.

levels.headline: The country did a bit better in July, but jobs are hard to find
levels.body:
Imagine your school fair. If lots of people come and buy cakes, the fair does well. In July, the UK did a bit better than people thought. More things were bought and sold in shops, cafes and hotels.
But some grown-ups do not have a job. Many of them want one. About 5 out of every 100 grown-ups who want a job cannot find one. That is a few more than last year.
So there is good news and not-so-good news. The country is doing better, but not everyone has work. Grown-ups hope that more jobs will come.
levels.why: When shops and businesses do well, there can be more jobs.

headline: Brent crude rises above $100 as stalled US-Iran talks raise supply fears

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil, named after a North Sea oil field
A narrow sea route at the mouth of the Gulf through which about a fifth of the world's oil passes
Using ships or force to stop goods or people reaching a place

levels.headline: Brent crude rises above $100 as stalled US-Iran talks raise supply fears
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose above $100 a barrel on Thursday 1 October as stalled talks between the United States and Iran raised fears of a longer conflict and further disruption to supplies. December Brent futures traded at about $100.49, up 2.5% on the previous close, and by one account closed up about 3.7% at around $101.62.
Prices were lifted by reports that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had asked an Iranian delegation, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to leave the United States after talks stalled. That weakened hopes of ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil flows. Iran says it has received Washington's response to a new proposal passed through Qatar, and sets out conditions including an end to fighting on all fronts including Lebanon, the lifting of the US naval blockade and the release of Iranian assets.
Oil has already pushed up UK inflation through petrol and diesel, and expensive energy is a key reason central banks are raising or considering rate rises.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and food costs, and they influence inflation and interest rates worldwide.

levels.headline: Brent oil tops $100 a barrel as US-Iran talks stall
levels.body:
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose above $100 a barrel on Thursday as US-Iran talks stalled. December contracts traded at about $100.49, up 2.5%, and one report had them closing about 3.7% higher at around $101.62. Investors fear a longer conflict and more disruption to supplies.
Reports said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio asked an Iranian delegation, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to leave the US after talks stalled. That reduced hopes of ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. Iran says it received a US response to a new proposal sent through Qatar. Its conditions include an end to hostilities on all fronts, the lifting of the US naval blockade and the release of Iranian assets.
Dearer oil has already pushed up petrol and diesel prices and UK inflation, and it is one reason central banks are raising or weighing higher interest rates.
levels.why: Oil prices affect fuel, heating and food bills and the path of inflation and interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil goes above $100 a barrel as US and Iran talks stall
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the world's main oil price, went above $100 a barrel on Thursday. Talks between the US and Iran have stopped moving forward, and traders worry about a longer conflict and fewer supplies. December Brent traded at about $100.49, up 2.5%.
Reports said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio asked an Iranian delegation to leave the US. That lowered hopes of a deal to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's oil goes through this narrow sea route. Iran says it has the US reply to a proposal sent through Qatar. It wants fighting to end everywhere, the US naval blockade lifted and Iranian assets released.
Dearer oil has already pushed up petrol prices and UK inflation. It is also one reason banks are raising interest rates.
levels.why: Expensive oil raises fuel and energy bills and makes inflation harder to bring down.

levels.headline: The price of oil goes above $100 a barrel as talks between the US and Iran stall
levels.body:
Oil is sold in barrels. On Thursday, the price of Brent crude, the world's main oil price, went above $100 a barrel. It rose because talks between the US and Iran stopped making progress. People who buy and sell oil worry that the conflict will last longer and that less oil will get through.
Reports said that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio asked an Iranian group to leave the US. That made a peace deal seem less likely. A deal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that about a fifth of the world's oil sails through. Iran says it wants the fighting to stop everywhere, the US ships to stop blocking its ports and its money to be handed back.
When oil is dear, petrol and energy cost more. This has already pushed up prices in the UK.
levels.why: It makes petrol, heating and travel cost more.

levels.headline: Oil goes above $100 a barrel because talks between the US and Iran are stuck
levels.body:
Oil is sold in barrels. On Thursday, the price of Brent crude, the world's main oil price, went above $100 a barrel. It rose because talks between the US and Iran were stuck. Traders worry the conflict will last longer and that less oil will get through.
A fifth of the world's oil sails through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has made that route a worry. Reports said that a US leader asked an Iranian group to leave the US. That made a deal seem less likely. Iran says it wants the fighting to stop everywhere and the US ships that block its ports to go.
When oil is dear, petrol and energy cost more. This has already pushed up prices in the UK.
levels.why: It makes petrol, heating and travel cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs more than $100 a barrel because talks between two countries are stuck
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. It is sold in barrels. On Thursday, a barrel of the main kind of oil, called Brent, cost more than $100. The price went up because talks between the US and Iran are stuck.
A lot of the world's oil travels on ships through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. About one barrel in every five goes that way. Because of the conflict, that route is not working normally. A report said a US leader asked an Iranian group to leave the US. That made a deal seem less likely.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and so do heating and travel.
levels.why: It makes many everyday things cost more, such as petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil is getting very dear because two countries cannot agree
levels.body:
Many cars and lorries run on fuel made from oil. On Thursday the price of a barrel of oil went above $100. That is a lot. It went up because the US and Iran, two countries, are in a fight and talks have stopped.
Much of the world's oil goes on ships through a narrow sea path called the Strait of Hormuz. About one barrel in five goes that way. Because of the fight, the path is not working normally. Oil sellers worry that less oil will arrive.
When oil is dear, petrol is dear. Things that are moved by lorry cost more to deliver too, so some food and goods can cost more.
levels.why: When oil costs more, many things you buy can cost more too.

levels.headline: Oil costs more than $100 a barrel because two countries cannot agree
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol and diesel. It is sold in barrels, and a barrel now costs more than $100. The price rose on Thursday because the US and Iran, two countries in a fight, have stopped making progress in their talks.
Lots of oil travels by ship along a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. About one barrel in every five goes that way. Because of the conflict, people worry that less oil will arrive. When there is less of something, it costs more.
Dearer oil means dearer petrol. It also costs more to move food and goods by lorry, so some prices in shops can go up too.
levels.why: It makes lots of everyday things cost more, from petrol to some foods.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because two countries are in a fight
levels.body:
Oil makes cars, buses and planes go. It is sold in barrels, and a barrel now costs more than $100. That is more than a few weeks ago. The reason is that two countries, the US and Iran, are in a fight, and their talks to fix it have stopped.
A lot of oil sails on ships down a narrow sea road. If it is blocked, less oil gets to shops and petrol stations. Then it costs more. People are worried it could go on for a while.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more. Heating can cost more too. This is why grown-ups are watching the news about it.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and other things can cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is dear because grown-up countries cannot agree
levels.body:
Oil is something from under the ground that makes cars and buses go. Today a barrel of oil costs a lot. That is because two countries are cross with each other, and they have stopped talking about how to fix it.
Much oil travels on ships along a narrow sea road. If the fight makes that road unsafe, less oil gets through. When there is less of something, it costs more. It is like when everyone wants the last cake at a party.
When oil costs more, grown-ups pay more for petrol. Buses and lorries cost more to run too. That can make some things in the shop cost more.
levels.why: When oil is dear, many things can cost a bit more.

headline: US officials say Rubio ordered Iran's delegation out as peace talks stall; Tehran disputes the account

terms.meaning: Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a country's ports
When a neutral country or group helps two sides talk and reach agreement
An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time

levels.headline: US officials say Rubio ordered Iran's delegation out as peace talks stall; Tehran disputes the account
levels.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation to leave the United States, according to US officials cited by Axios, after talks aimed at ending the conflict deadlocked on Monday 28 September. One official said the delegation had "overstayed their welcome" because the UN General Assembly was over. Iran's UN mission says the departure had been planned in advance and communicated to the State Department on 17 September. The delegation left for the airport hours later and flew to Doha.
The talks are meant to end the war, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and revive negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme. Reports describe irreconcilable differences over the nuclear issue and the US naval blockade. Iran's government spokesperson said Tehran had received a US response to a new proposal sent through Qatari mediation, with conditions including an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon, the lifting of the blockade and the release of Iranian assets.
Reuters reported on 1 October that Iran was readying a harder response if attacked and that diplomacy faced long odds, while the two sides largely agree on the steps but not their order. Oil rose above $100 a barrel on the news.
levels.why: The stalled talks keep the Strait of Hormuz at risk and are pushing up oil prices and inflation worldwide.

levels.headline: US and Iran talks stall as Rubio reportedly tells Iranian delegation to leave
levels.body:
US officials say Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his delegation to leave the United States after talks deadlocked on Monday. A US official said they had "overstayed their welcome" now that the UN General Assembly was over. Iran says the departure had been planned and told to the State Department on 17 September. The group flew to Doha.
The talks aim to end the conflict, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart discussions on Iran's nuclear programme. They are stuck over the nuclear issue and the US naval blockade. Iran says it has the US reply to a new proposal passed via Qatar. It wants hostilities to end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the blockade lifted and Iranian assets released.
On 1 October Reuters reported that Iran was preparing a tougher response if attacked and that the two sides largely agree on the steps but not their order. Oil rose above $100 a barrel.
levels.why: The deadlock keeps oil prices high and adds to worries about inflation.

levels.headline: Talks between the US and Iran stall, and the two sides tell different stories
levels.body:
US officials say that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his team to leave the country after talks got stuck on Monday. One official said they had "overstayed their welcome". Iran says the team's departure was already planned and that it told the US on 17 September. The team flew on to Doha.
The talks are meant to end the conflict, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart discussion of Iran's nuclear programme. The sides disagree about the nuclear issue and the US navy blockade of Iran. Iran says it wants fighting to end everywhere, including Lebanon, the blockade lifted and its assets released.
Reuters reported that the two sides largely agree on what steps to take but not in what order. The oil price rose above $100 a barrel.
levels.why: If talks fail, oil stays expensive and prices keep rising around the world.

levels.headline: US and Iran peace talks are stuck, and each side tells a different story
levels.body:
US officials say Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his team to leave the US after talks got stuck on Monday. They said the team had stayed too long after a big UN meeting. Iran says the team's trip home was planned long before, and that it told the US on 17 September. The team flew to Qatar.
The talks are meant to end the conflict, open up a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, and restart talks about Iran's nuclear programme. The two sides disagree about the nuclear issue and about the US ships that block Iran's ports. Iran also wants fighting to stop in all places, including Lebanon.
One report says both sides agree on what needs to happen but not on what should come first. Oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel.
levels.why: When talks fail, oil and petrol stay expensive for everyone.

levels.headline: The US and Iran cannot agree, and talks have stopped moving
levels.body:
The US and Iran are in a conflict. Leaders have been trying to talk to end it. This week the talks got stuck. US officials say the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, told Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his team to leave the US. Iran says they were always planning to leave on that day. Each side tells the story differently.
The talks are about stopping the fighting, opening a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's nuclear programme. The two sides disagree about the nuclear plans and about US ships that block Iran's ports. Iran also wants fighting to stop everywhere.
Both sides seem to agree about what needs to happen, but not about which step should come first. Because of this, the price of oil has gone up.
levels.why: The talks decide whether oil gets cheaper and whether the conflict ends.

levels.headline: Talks between the US and Iran are stuck, and each side tells it differently
levels.body:
The US and Iran are in a conflict. This week the talks to end it got stuck. US officials say the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, told Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his team to leave the US. Iran says they were always planning to leave that day, and that it told the US on 17 September.
The talks are about three things: stopping the fighting, opening a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's nuclear programme. The sides disagree about the nuclear plans and about US ships that block Iran's ports.
Both sides seem to agree on what needs to be done, but not on which step comes first. The price of oil has gone above $100 a barrel because of this.
levels.why: The talks decide whether oil gets cheaper and whether the conflict ends.

levels.headline: Talks to end a fight between two countries have got stuck
levels.body:
The US and Iran are two countries in a fight. They have been talking to try to end it. This week the talks got stuck. The US says its leader for talks, Marco Rubio, asked Iran's team to leave the country. Iran says the team was always going to leave that day. Each side tells the story in a different way.
They are trying to agree about three things. First, to stop the fighting. Second, to open a sea road that many oil ships use. Third, what to do about Iran's nuclear plans. A nuclear plan is about very powerful weapons and energy. They do not agree on this.
It seems both sides want similar things but not in the same order. The price of oil has gone up because of this.
levels.why: If the fighting continues, oil stays expensive and prices rise.

levels.headline: Two countries have stopped talking about how to end their fight
levels.body:
The US and Iran are two countries that are fighting. People from both sides have been talking about how to stop it. But this week the talking stopped working. The US says it asked the Iranian team to go home. Iran says the team was going home anyway. They tell the story in different ways.
They are talking about stopping the fighting and about a sea road that oil ships use. They also talk about very powerful weapons that Iran may try to make. They do not agree, and they have not decided who goes first.
Because of this, the price of oil has gone up. This means petrol can cost more.
levels.why: When countries cannot agree, oil gets dearer and things in shops cost more.

levels.headline: Two countries have stopped talking to each other for now
levels.body:
Imagine two friends who are cross with each other. They sit down to talk. After a while, they get stuck, because each wants the other to say sorry first. This is what has happened with the US and Iran. They are two countries in a fight. Their talks have stopped.
Each side says something a bit different about what happened. They both want the fighting to stop. But they cannot agree who should go first. A sea road that many oil ships use is also in the middle of the fight.
Because of this, oil costs more. Petrol can cost more too. Grown-ups hope the countries will talk again soon.
levels.why: When people cannot agree, it can make things dearer for everyone.

levels.headline: Two countries are cross and have stopped talking
levels.body:
Sometimes two friends have a fight and stop talking. Then a grown-up helps them talk. Two countries called the US and Iran are in a fight. Some people from both sides sat down to talk. But they got stuck. Each says something a bit different about what happened.
They both want the fight to end. But each wants the other to do something first. It is a bit like both of them waiting for the other to say sorry.
This matters to everyone because oil ships sail near these countries. When there is a fight, oil costs more. Grown-ups hope the two countries will start talking again.
levels.why: When countries fight, many people far away feel it in the price of things.

headline: US employers add only 29,000 jobs in September, far below forecasts, as unemployment rises to 4.2%

terms.meaning: The number of paid jobs in the economy, counted each month
The central bank of the United States, which sets its main interest rate
The share of adults who are working or looking for work

levels.headline: US employers add only 29,000 jobs in September, far below forecasts, as unemployment rises to 4.2%
levels.body:
US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, well below the 84,000 economists had expected, according to figures published on Friday 2 October. That is a sharp slowdown from August, when 162,000 jobs were first reported.
The figures were also revised. August was cut to 133,000, and July changed from a gain to a loss of 10,000 jobs, so revisions removed 60,000 jobs in total. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, largely because more people joined the labour force, and participation reached a four-month high of 61.8%. Average hourly earnings rose only 0.1% on the month and 3% on a year earlier, the slowest annual pace since 2021.
Financial markets reacted at once. S&P 500 futures rose, while Treasury yields and the dollar fell, as traders trimmed bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this year. The Fed raised its main rate on 16 September, its first rise since July 2023, as oil prices pushed inflation up.
levels.why: US job figures steer interest rates, and US rates influence borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: US job growth slows sharply in September as unemployment rises to 4.2%
levels.body:
The US economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, far fewer than the 84,000 forecast, the government said on Friday 2 October. In August the first estimate had been 162,000.
Earlier months were revised down as well. August is now 133,000 and July became a fall of 10,000, which together take 60,000 jobs off the previous total. Unemployment rose to 4.2%, mainly because more people were looking for work. Pay is growing slowly: hourly earnings were up 0.1% on the month and 3% on the year, the weakest annual rise since 2021.
Markets took it as a sign that the Federal Reserve may not need to raise rates again soon. US stock futures rose and the dollar and Treasury yields fell. The Fed raised rates on 16 September for the first time since 2023 because oil was pushing up prices.
levels.why: A weaker jobs market makes more rate rises less likely, which affects borrowing costs everywhere.

levels.headline: US employers hire far fewer people than expected in September
levels.body:
US employers took on only 29,000 more workers in September. Experts had expected about 84,000. The government published the figures on Friday 2 October. In August the first figure had been 162,000.
Some earlier numbers were lowered too. August was cut to 133,000 jobs, and July turned into a loss of 10,000. Altogether that is 60,000 fewer jobs than first reported. The unemployment rate went up to 4.2%, mostly because more people started looking for work. Wages grew by just 0.1% in the month and by 3% over the year, the slowest rise since 2021.
Investors reacted quickly. Stock futures rose, while the dollar and the interest rate on US government debt fell. Traders now think the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, is less likely to raise its interest rate again this year. It last raised it on 16 September.
levels.why: It shows whether the US economy is slowing, and that affects interest rates and prices worldwide.

levels.headline: The US jobs market slows down: only 29,000 new jobs in September
levels.body:
US employers added 29,000 jobs in September. That is much lower than the 84,000 experts expected. The news came out on Friday 2 October. In August, the first number was 162,000, so this is a big drop.
Some older numbers were made smaller too. August is now 133,000 jobs. July shows a loss of 10,000 jobs. The share of people without a job went up to 4.2%, partly because more people began looking for work. Pay is rising slowly, up 3% over the year. That is the slowest since 2021.
The stock market and the bond market both noticed. Share prices for the big US firms looked set to rise. The dollar and the interest rate on US government debt went down. Investors now think the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, may not raise its interest rate again this year.
levels.why: It affects whether US interest rates go up, which changes borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: Fewer new jobs in the US than people expected
levels.body:
The US government counts how many new jobs there are each month. In September there were only 29,000 new ones. Experts had thought there would be about 84,000. The numbers came out on Friday 2 October.
The government also changed some earlier numbers to make them smaller. This means the jobs market has been weaker than people thought. The share of people without a job rose to 4.2%. Pay is going up only slowly, by about 3% in a year.
This matters to the Federal Reserve, the US central bank. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It raised the rate on 16 September because prices were rising. Now investors think it may not need to raise it again soon. Share prices rose a little, and the dollar went down.
levels.why: Job numbers help decide interest rates, which change what loans cost.

levels.headline: US job growth drops sharply, with only 29,000 new jobs in September
levels.body:
The US counts how many new jobs are created every month. In September the number was just 29,000. Experts had expected about 84,000, so it was a big disappointment. The figures came out on Friday 2 October.
Some earlier figures were lowered too, which means the jobs market was weaker than people believed. More people are now without work: 4.2% of those who want a job. Pay is rising slowly, only about 3% over a year, the slowest since 2021.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It raised the rate on 16 September because prices were going up. After this news, investors think it may not raise it again soon. Share prices rose a little and the dollar fell.
levels.why: It helps decide whether borrowing gets dearer, in the US and elsewhere.

levels.headline: The US adds far fewer jobs than expected
levels.body:
Each month, the US counts how many new jobs have been made. In September the number was 29,000. That is small. People who study money had guessed about 84,000. The numbers came out on Friday 2 October.
Some numbers from earlier months were made smaller too. So the jobs market is weaker than people thought. More people are without a job now: 4.2% of people who want to work. Wages are rising slowly. That means people's pay packets are growing only a little.
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It put the rate up on 16 September because prices in shops were rising. Now fewer people think it will go up again soon. Share prices rose a little on the news.
levels.why: Fewer jobs can mean the central bank holds off on putting up interest rates.

levels.headline: Not many new jobs were made in the US last month
levels.body:
Every month, the US counts the new jobs that were made. Last month there were only 29,000. That is far fewer than people expected. A job is when someone is paid to work. The count came out on Friday 2 October.
The US also made some old numbers smaller. This shows the jobs market is not as strong as people thought. A few more people are without a job now. Pay is going up slowly, so shopping money does not stretch much further.
The US has a big bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It decides how dear it is to borrow money. It made borrowing dearer on 16 September, because prices in shops were going up. After this news, people think it will not do that again soon. Share prices went up a little.
levels.why: It helps decide whether borrowing gets dearer or cheaper.

levels.headline: Fewer new jobs than people hoped for in the US
levels.body:
Last month, only 29,000 new jobs were made in the US. People had thought there would be many more. A job is work that you get paid for. The news came out on Friday 2 October.
It means some workplaces are not hiring as many people as before. Pay is going up only slowly too. A few more people are looking for work and cannot find it yet.
The country has a big bank that sets the price of borrowing money. It is called the Federal Reserve. Last month it made borrowing a bit dearer, because things in shops cost more. Now people think it may wait. If it waits, borrowing may stop getting dearer. Share prices went up a little when people heard the news.
levels.why: It may stop borrowing from getting dearer.

levels.headline: There were not many new jobs last month
levels.body:
Imagine a town where some shops want to hire helpers. Last month, far fewer shops hired helpers than people hoped. This happened in the US, which is a very big country. A new job means a new helper who gets paid.
Because fewer shops hired, a few more people are looking for a job. Pay is also growing slowly, like pocket money that goes up by just a few pence.
The country has a big bank that decides how dear it is to borrow money. Last month it made it a bit dearer, because prices in shops were going up. Now people think it may wait and not make it dearer again. Some grown-ups who buy and sell shares felt happy about that, and share prices went up a little.
levels.why: It could stop borrowing money from getting dearer.

headline: US 10-year Treasury yield reaches highest since 2002 as Wall Street finishes flat

terms.meaning: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow; it also guides many other borrowing costs
The central bank of the United States, which sets its main interest rate
An index of 500 large US companies, used as a measure of the US stock market

levels.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield reaches highest since 2002 as Wall Street finishes flat
levels.body:
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose 4 basis points to about 5.33% on Thursday 1 October, its highest since April 2002, while the 30-year yield rose to about 5.67%, the highest since July 2002. Yields touched an intraday peak of 5.344% before turning lower in late-morning trading.
US stocks recovered from early losses to finish slightly higher on the first trading day of October. The S&P 500 rose 0.19% to 7,666.45, the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.04% to 26,871.60 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 20.51 points, or 0.04%, to 50,926.56, helped by AI-related and chip shares. Some live reports described the market as dipping earlier in the day.
The Federal Reserve raised its main rate by 0.25 points to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on 16 September, its first rise since July 2023, and signalled that another could follow, as oil prices push inflation up. Higher US yields tend to push up borrowing costs elsewhere, which is part of the pressure on UK gilts.
levels.why: US borrowing costs set the tone for mortgages, company loans and government debt around the world.

levels.headline: US government borrowing costs hit a 24-year high, but shares end the day flat
levels.body:
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury rose 4 basis points to about 5.33% on Thursday, the highest since April 2002. The 30-year yield rose to about 5.67%, the highest since July 2002. Yields reached an intraday high of 5.344% and then eased in the late morning.
Wall Street recovered from early falls to end slightly higher. The S&P 500 rose 0.19% to 7,666.45, the Nasdaq rose 0.04% to 26,871.60 and the Dow gained 20.51 points to 50,926.56. Gains in AI-related and chip shares helped.
The Federal Reserve raised its main rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on 16 September, its first rise since July 2023, and signalled another may follow because oil prices are pushing up inflation. Higher US yields tend to lift borrowing costs elsewhere, including the UK.
levels.why: Rising US yields push up the cost of borrowing in many countries.

levels.headline: US borrowing costs reach their highest in over 20 years, while shares end flat
levels.body:
The interest rate on 10-year US government debt rose to about 5.33% on Thursday. It is the highest since April 2002. The rate on 30-year debt rose to about 5.67%, the highest since July 2002. Both eased a little later in the morning from their highest points.
Share prices in the US bounced back from early losses to finish about the same. The S&P 500 rose 0.19%, the Nasdaq rose 0.04% and the Dow rose 0.04%. Shares in AI and chip companies helped.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised its main interest rate on 16 September to between 3.75% and 4.00%. It was the first rise since July 2023, and it hinted that another could come because oil prices are pushing up inflation. When US rates rise, borrowing often gets dearer in other countries too.
levels.why: What happens to US interest rates affects loans and prices around the world.

levels.headline: The US government is paying its highest interest rates for over 20 years
levels.body:
The US government borrows money by selling debt called Treasuries. The interest rate on 10-year Treasuries rose to about 5.33% on Thursday, the highest since 2002. For 30-year ones it was about 5.67%. Rates dipped a little later in the morning.
On the stock market, share prices ended the day about the same. They had fallen early on and then recovered. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big US companies, rose 0.19%. Shares in AI and computer chip firms helped.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised its main interest rate on 16 September to between 3.75% and 4.00%. This was the first rise since July 2023. It also hinted that another rise could come, because oil prices are pushing up prices in the shops. Higher US rates often make borrowing dearer in other countries too.
levels.why: US interest rates affect borrowing costs and prices all over the world.

levels.headline: US government borrowing is the most expensive it has been since 2002
levels.body:
Governments borrow money by selling bonds. In the US they are called Treasuries. The interest on 10-year Treasuries went up to about 5.33% on Thursday. That is the highest since 2002. Interest on 30-year ones went to about 5.67%.
Share prices in the US ended the day about the same as before. They dropped early on and then bounced back. Shares in AI and computer chip companies did well.
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate. On 16 September it raised the rate to between 3.75% and 4.00%. That was the first rise since July 2023. It said another may come, because oil is dear and prices are rising. When US rates go up, other countries often have to pay more to borrow too.
levels.why: Costs in the US can spread to other countries, including loans in the UK.

levels.headline: It costs the US government more to borrow than it has for over 20 years
levels.body:
Countries borrow money, just like families do. The US government pays interest to the people who lend to it. On Thursday the interest it pays on a 10-year loan went up to about 5.33%. That is the highest since 2002.
Share prices stayed about the same. A share is a small piece of a company. Prices fell in the morning and then went back up. Companies that make computer chips and AI did well.
The US has a special bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It sets a main interest rate. On 16 September it put the rate up a little, to between 3.75% and 4.00%. It said it might do so again, because oil is dear and prices are rising. When this happens in the US, borrowing can get dearer elsewhere too.
levels.why: Higher costs to borrow in the US can make borrowing dearer in other countries as well.

levels.headline: Borrowing is getting dearer for the US government
levels.body:
The US government borrows lots of money. It pays interest to the people who lend it. On Thursday the interest went up to its highest level for more than 20 years. That means borrowing is getting dearer.
Share prices stayed about the same on the day. A share is a tiny piece of a company. They went down early and then up again. Companies that make computer chips did well.
The US has a bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It sets a main interest rate. Last month it made that rate a bit higher. It said it might do so again, because oil is dear and prices are rising. When this happens in the US, it can make borrowing dearer in other countries too.
levels.why: It can make loans cost more all over the world.

levels.headline: The US has to pay more interest to borrow
levels.body:
Think of a big country borrowing pocket money from lots of people. It must pay them back with extra. The extra is called interest. This week the extra grew to its biggest size for over 20 years.
The country has a special bank that sets the main amount of extra. It is called the Federal Reserve. Last month it made the amount a little bigger. It might do it again. This is because oil is dear, and prices in shops are going up.
Share prices stayed about the same. A share is a tiny piece of a company. When the US pays more interest, other countries can end up paying more too.
levels.why: When the US pays more to borrow, others can end up paying more too.

levels.headline: The US country has to pay more for borrowing money
levels.body:
Do you borrow a pencil from a friend? You give it back. Countries borrow money, and they give it back with a little extra. The extra is called interest. This week, the US had to promise a bigger extra than it has for a very long time.
The country has a special bank that decides how big the extra should be. Last month it made it a little bigger. It might do it again soon, because prices in the shops are going up.
Share prices stayed about the same on the day. That means the companies were worth about the same. Grown-ups are watching, because what happens in the US can change things in other countries too.
levels.why: What big countries do with money can change things in other countries.

levels.headline: A big country pays more to borrow
levels.body:
A big country needs lots of money. Sometimes it borrows it. The people who lend want a thank-you in return, a little extra money. This extra is called interest. This week the extra got bigger. It is the biggest in over 20 years.
Think about borrowing sweets from a friend. If you promise to give back two extra, that is a lot. The country is a bit like that.
Grown-ups are watching, because other countries might have to give a bigger thank-you too. If they do, they have less money left for things like roads and schools.
levels.why: It can change how much money countries have left for roads and schools.

headline: Euro area inflation reached 3.3% in August, and the ECB has already raised rates

terms.meaning: The countries in Europe that use the euro as their currency
The ECB's main interest rate, paid to banks that park money with it
An early, quick figure published before the final numbers are ready

levels.headline: Euro area inflation reached 3.3% in August, and the ECB has already raised rates
levels.body:
Annual inflation in the euro area rose to 3.3% in August 2026, according to Eurostat's flash estimate published on 1 September, up from 2.9% in July by the agency's earlier releases. CNBC described it as back above 3% and said higher interest rates were likely to follow.
The European Central Bank then raised its main interest rates by 0.25 points at its meeting on 10 September, lifting the deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%, according to reports. The move came as energy costs surged because of the conflict involving Iran and disruption to oil supplies, and as underlying price pressures stayed firm.
Eurostat's flash estimate for September is due on 2 October. The US Federal Reserve has also raised rates and the Bank of England held its rate on 17 September with three members voting for a rise, so the main central banks are leaning towards tighter policy. For households in the euro area, that means dearer energy and more costly loans.
levels.why: It shows central banks around the world are tightening policy to fight energy-driven inflation.

levels.headline: Euro area inflation hits 3.3% and the European Central Bank has raised rates
levels.body:
Prices in the euro area were 3.3% higher in August than a year earlier, Eurostat's flash estimate showed on 1 September. That was up from 2.9% in July. CNBC said inflation was back above 3% and that higher interest rates were likely to follow.
The European Central Bank raised its main rates by 0.25 points at its meeting on 10 September, taking the deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.5%, reports said. Energy costs have surged because of the Iran conflict, and underlying price pressures have stayed firm.
Eurostat's flash estimate for September comes out on 2 October. The US Federal Reserve has also raised rates, and three Bank of England members voted for a rise in September, so the major central banks are leaning towards tighter policy. That means costlier loans for households and firms in the euro area.
levels.why: Central banks are raising rates to fight energy-driven inflation, and that makes borrowing dearer.

levels.headline: Prices rose 3.3% across the euro area in August, and interest rates went up
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro were 3.3% higher in August than a year before. This comes from Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, which published an early estimate on 1 September. In July the figure was 2.9%. The business broadcaster CNBC said inflation was back above 3% and that higher interest rates were likely.
The European Central Bank then raised its main rates by 0.25 points on 10 September, according to reports. The deposit rate went from 2.25% to 2.5%. Energy has become much dearer because of the conflict involving Iran.
A new early estimate for September is due on 2 October. The US central bank has also raised rates, and the Bank of England nearly did. So big central banks are all leaning towards higher rates. That means loans cost more for people and businesses.
levels.why: It means loans and mortgages are getting dearer across Europe, and it shows the problem is global.

levels.headline: Euro area prices rose 3.3% in a year, so the central bank put up interest rates
levels.body:
In the countries that use the euro, prices in August were 3.3% higher than a year before. In July the rise had been 2.9%. The figure comes from Eurostat, which counts prices for the EU. A news site said inflation was back above 3% and that rates were likely to go up.
The European Central Bank is the bank for these countries. On 10 September it raised its main rate, the deposit rate, from 2.25% to 2.5%. Energy has become much dearer because of the conflict involving Iran, so prices have risen.
New figures for September are due today. The US central bank has also put up rates. The Bank of England kept its rate the same but three voters wanted a rise. So loans are likely to stay costly.
levels.why: It means loans cost more and shows that high energy prices are causing problems in many countries.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe rose 3.3% in a year, so a big bank raised interest rates
levels.body:
In the countries that use the euro, prices in August were 3.3% higher than a year before. In July the rise was 2.9%. The numbers come from Eurostat, which counts prices for the EU. A news site said inflation was back above 3% and that rates were likely to rise.

levels.body:
A Russian drone struck a school building in the Solomianskyi district of Kyiv on Thursday 1 October, starting a fire. More than 100 children and over 60 teachers were in shelters inside at the time. Ukrainian authorities said the drone's 50 kilogram warhead pierced the floor but did not explode, and no casualties were reported.
Photographs showed a large hole in the brick facade, burn marks and smashed windows. President Volodymyr Zelensky called Russian strikes on schools and kindergartens "a deliberate tactic" aimed at ordinary life, and said Ukraine needed additional missiles in October to defend itself.
The attack is part of Russia's continuing aerial campaign against Ukraine, now in its fifth year, with Kyiv targeted by drones and missiles at almost every opportunity. Schools and shelters are central to daily life in the capital, where lessons often continue underground during alerts. Russia has repeatedly said that it targets military sites, a claim Ukraine and its allies reject. The strike came on the same day Russia expelled Hungarian diplomats.

headline: Greece asks the EU to allow asylum applications to be suspended during migration emergencies

levels.headline: Greece asks the EU to allow asylum applications to be suspended during migration emergencies
levels.body:
Greece urged the European Union on Thursday 1 October to let member states temporarily suspend asylum applications during major migration flows, arguing that current rules are inadequate for mass arrivals such as those seen this summer in Ceuta, Spain's North African enclave. The proposal was put to EU interior ministers meeting in Luxembourg for the Justice and Home Affairs Council.
Greece wants it included in the "European Emergency Response Framework", a new law the European Commission will present in the coming months. If triggered, the mechanism would allow temporary suspension of asylum applications, accelerated return procedures and immediate help from the EU border agency Frontex. Some member states appeared sympathetic, and Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said: "We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure."
Left-wing politicians, migration experts and civil society groups criticised the idea, saying that suspending a fundamental right would be unprecedented and could undermine existing safeguards. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said that international law had to be respected when asked whether a suspension was possible.
levels.why: It could change how Europe treats people seeking protection and tests the limits of refugee law.

levels.headline: Greece proposes that the EU be able to pause asylum claims in emergencies

On Thursday Greece asked the EU to let countries temporarily suspend asylum applications during big migration surges. It said the current rules do not work for mass arrivals, citing events in Ceuta, Spain's enclave in North Africa, this summer. It put the idea to EU interior ministers in Luxembourg.
Greece wants the power added to the "European Emergency Response Framework", a law the European Commission plans to present in the coming months. In a crisis it would allow a pause on asylum applications, faster returns and immediate help from the border agency Frontex. Some countries seemed to agree. The Dutch migration minister, Bart van den Brink, said the aim was to find a legal way not to bring people into the asylum procedure.
Left-wing politicians and rights groups say suspending a basic right would be unprecedented and risky. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said international law must be respected.
levels.why: It could change how Europe treats people who seek protection, and raises legal and moral questions.

levels.why: It could change how Europe treats people seeking safety.

headline: Russia expels Hungarian diplomats in retaliation for Budapest's expulsion of 10 Russian envoys

levels.headline: Russia expels Hungarian diplomats in retaliation for Budapest's expulsion of 10 Russian envoys
levels.body:
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday 1 October that it would expel an unspecified number of Hungarian diplomats in a tit-for-tat move. Staff from Hungary's embassy in Moscow and its consulates in St Petersburg and Kazan have been declared personae non gratae and given two weeks to leave. Moscow did not say how many are affected, although such retaliation usually matches the original number.
The step follows Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán's announcement on 8 September that Budapest was expelling 10 Russian diplomats for activities incompatible with their status. Russia summoned Hungary's chargé d'affaires, Gábor Gergics, to deliver a "decisive protest" over what it called a "groundless and openly unfriendly" decision.
Hungary said it stood by its decision, taken on national security grounds, and that its missions in Russia remain fully operational and it will keep a diplomatic presence. Reports describe the dispute as a sign of Budapest breaking with the policies of the Orbán era, when Hungary kept closer ties to Moscow than most EU members.
levels.why: It shows relations between Russia and a member of the EU and NATO are deteriorating.

headline: Bosnia and Herzegovina goes to the polls on 4 October with new anti-fraud technology

levels.headline: Bosnia and Herzegovina goes to the polls on 4 October with new anti-fraud technology
levels.body:
Bosnia and Herzegovina holds general elections on Sunday 4 October, with about 3.4 million registered voters, of whom about 48,000 are abroad. Voters will choose the country's three-member Presidency, parliaments at state and entity level, and other offices, including the 98-member House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the assemblies of the Federation's ten cantons.
It is the first general election to use new technology designed to reduce fraud, a long-running concern in the country's elections. Analysts describe the contest, especially the battle for the Presidency, as being about the model of governance, with commentators weighing "opportunity for change" against "continued fragmentation" in a political system shaped by the 1995 Dayton peace agreement and divided between ethnic groups.
A Reuters report on 1 October described foreign powers jostling for influence ahead of the vote. The result will matter for the country's bid to join the EU and for how it handles internal tensions.
levels.why: The election will show whether Bosnia's divided politics can change and how close it moves to the EU.

levels.headline: Bosnia and Herzegovina votes on 4 October for its Presidency and parliaments

They will choose the three-member Presidency, state and entity parliaments, the 98-member Federation House of Representatives and the assemblies of the Federation's ten cantons.
It is the first national election to use new technology meant to cut fraud, which has been a long-running worry. Analysts say the fight for the Presidency is about how the country should be governed, and they weigh a chance for change against more of the same division in a political system based on the 1995 Dayton peace agreement and split between ethnic groups.

levels.body:

levels.headline: A country will choose its leaders on Sunday
levels.body:

They will use new computer tools to make sure the vote is fair. A fair vote means that everyone follows the rules and nobody cheats.
After the vote, the people who win will help to run the country. They make rules and look after things that everybody shares, like roads and schools.
levels.why: Voting lets people choose the leaders they want.
